title: Asset Allocation and the Alternatives Sleeve
summary: The allocation decision explains most of a portfolio's outcome, and the optimiser that produces it is fed inputs that guarantee more private assets.

lesson.body:
Asset allocation is the decision about how much to hold of each broad exposure. It comes before manager selection and it matters more.

The conventional process has three steps:

**Capital market assumptions.** Expected return, volatility and correlation for each asset class. All three are estimates; the first is nearly unknowable and the other two are measured on history.

**Optimisation or judgement.** A mean-variance optimiser, a risk-parity approach, or a committee. All produce weights.

**Constraints.** Liquidity needs, policy limits, governance tolerance, regulatory requirements.

**The third step usually determines the answer, and it is treated as an afterthought.** An optimiser without constraints recommends portfolios no institution could hold; with realistic constraints, the optimisation is mostly choosing between a small number of feasible options.

Which is worth knowing before spending weeks on the inputs. **The high-value work in allocation is defining the constraints honestly** — what liquidity is genuinely needed, what drawdown the governance can survive, what the actual time horizon is — because those decide the outcome.

**A mean-variance optimiser fed private market statistics will always recommend more private assets, and the recommendation comes from the measurement rather than from the economics.**

The mechanism, from the marks topic: private returns are quarterly estimates that adjust partway toward reality. That smoothing produces:

**Understated volatility** — often half the true figure or less.

**Understated correlation** with public markets.

**Overstated [[sharpe-ratio|Sharpe ratios]]**, because volatility sits in the denominator.

An optimiser rewards exactly those three properties. It has no way to know one series was estimated and another was traded, so it allocates accordingly. **The output is not an investment conclusion; it is the smoothing, restated as a recommendation.**

Three corrections, in order of preference:

**Unsmooth the private return series** using its autocorrelation, and re-run. Standard technique, rarely applied.

**Substitute a lagged public proxy** — levered small-cap for buyout, levered loans for [[private-credit|private credit]] — and use its statistics.

**Apply an explicit volatility haircut** and document it. Crude, transparent, and far better than nothing.

**And then impose the liquidity constraint separately**, because an optimiser has no concept of not being able to sell.

**The case for an alternatives allocation is not that it produces higher returns. It is that it accesses return sources a public portfolio cannot.**

Stated plainly, there are four:

**The illiquidity premium.** Compensation for accepting that you cannot sell. Real, and only earned by investors who genuinely do not need to sell — for anyone else it is a risk taken without the corresponding payment.

**Access to a different opportunity set.** Most companies are private. Some sectors and stages exist only there.

**Control and influence.** A buyout owner can change management, [[capital-structure|capital structure]] and strategy. A minority public shareholder cannot.

**Genuinely different payoff shapes.** Trend following and some macro strategies behave unlike everything else, and that is worth more than their standalone returns suggest.

**What is not on the list: lower volatility.** That is a measurement artefact. Nor is "diversification" in the abstract — [[private-equity|private equity]] is levered equity, and its true correlation with public equity is high once the smoothing is removed.

**So the honest sizing question is: how much illiquidity can this portfolio genuinely bear, given its liabilities and its governance?** That number is a liquidity calculation rather than an optimisation, and it is the binding constraint for almost every institution.

lesson.caption: What each allocation actually buys
rows: Equity premium plus leverage plus illiquidity
Ten-year [[lockup|lock-up]], fees, and correlation you cannot measure honestly.
Lock-up, and credit deterioration that appears late.
Capital intensity, and sensitivity to long rates.
A payoff shape opposite to the rest
Losing money most of the time, which is what makes it work.
The only reliable diversifier in a [[deleveraging]]
The lowest expected return, which is why it gets minimised.

lesson.body: An optimiser is given two candidate assets. Public equity: 8% expected return, 16% volatility. A private strategy: 10% expected return, 8% reported volatility, correlation 0.4 with equities.
walkthrough: On those inputs the private strategy dominates: higher return, half the volatility, low correlation. **An unconstrained optimiser allocates heavily to it.**
Now unsmooth. The private series has high autocorrelation; correcting it gives roughly **16% volatility** and a correlation nearer **0.75**.

**Read that carefully: on the corrected inputs the private strategy is levered equity with a 2% return advantage and a lock-up.** That is a defensible allocation and a completely different one from what the optimiser first proposed.
The Sharpe ratio moves the same way. At a 3% [[risk-free-rate|risk-free rate]]: reported (10 − 3)/8 = **0.88**; corrected (10 − 3)/16 = **0.44**. Public equity is (8 − 3)/16 = **0.31**.
So the private strategy still wins on the corrected figures — by a sensible margin rather than an implausible one.
**And the sizing constraint is now the lock-up rather than the optimiser**, which is the honest place for it to sit.

Sanity check worth reusing: **before any optimisation involving private assets, compute the autocorrelation of each private return series.** A high figure means the inputs need correcting, and the correction changes the answer rather than refining it.

lesson.body:
**Optimising on smoothed inputs.** The single largest error in institutional allocation, and it is invisible because the arithmetic is correct.

**Expected returns extrapolated from the recent past.** A decade of falling rates produced excellent returns for long-duration and levered assets. Assuming that continues is a rate forecast disguised as an assumption.

**Constraints applied after optimisation.** Optimise first, then constrain, and the result is an unconstrained portfolio trimmed to fit. Better to define the feasible set first.

**Ignoring the fee difference in expected returns.** A 10% gross private return with 2-and-20 is not 10%. Comparisons have to be net of everything, and the gross figure is what usually appears in the assumptions.

**Rebalancing rules that cannot be executed.** A policy requiring quarterly rebalancing to target cannot rebalance illiquid assets, so it rebalances the liquid ones — which changes the portfolio in ways nobody chose.

**Treating a target as achievable immediately.** A private markets target takes years to reach through commitments, so the portfolio spends most of its life away from its target by construction.

**The binding constraint on most institutional portfolios is not liquidity or risk tolerance. It is what the governing body will tolerate seeing.**

This is rarely written down and it decides outcomes. A committee that will not sit through a 25% drawdown has an effective stop-loss at 25%, whether or not a document says so. A portfolio built on a twenty-year horizon and reviewed against annual benchmarks is being managed to one year.

The mismatch produces predictable behaviour:

**Selling at the bottom.** Not because the strategy failed, but because the drawdown exceeded tolerance.

**Chasing recent performance.** Allocating to whatever has worked, which is a decision about the last cycle.

**Manager turnover at the worst time.** Terminating after three bad years, which for most strategies is a normal sample.

**Illiquidity as a commitment device.** The uncomfortable truth is that a lock-up prevents the panic sale — which is part of why private market returns have exceeded public ones for the same investors. Some of the illiquidity premium is compensation for a constraint, and some of it is protection from ourselves.

**So the honest allocation process states the governance tolerance as an explicit constraint** — "we can survive a 20% drawdown and not a 35% one" — and builds within it. **A portfolio the committee cannot hold through a bad year is not a long-horizon portfolio, whatever the policy says.**

**Compute the autocorrelation of every private return series before it enters an optimiser.** A high figure means the inputs need unsmoothing first.

**Ask what the allocation looks like with private volatility doubled and correlation raised to 0.75.** That is the honest input set, and the answer is the defensible allocation.

**State the governance drawdown tolerance explicitly and build within it.** An unstated tolerance operates as a stop-loss nobody chose.

**Check that expected returns are net of all fees.** Gross private returns compared with net public ones systematically favour the private allocation.

**Ask how the rebalancing policy handles illiquid assets.** If it cannot rebalance them, it is a policy for rebalancing the liquid portfolio — which is a different decision.

items: Constraints usually determine the allocation, so defining them honestly is the high-value work — not refining the expected return assumptions.
An optimiser fed smoothed private statistics always recommends more private assets: unsmoothing took a strategy from 8% to 16% volatility and 0.4 to 0.75 correlation.
Alternatives buy the illiquidity premium, a different opportunity set, control, and different payoff shapes. They do not buy lower volatility — that is a measurement artefact.
The binding constraint is usually governance tolerance. A portfolio the committee cannot hold through a bad year is not a long-horizon portfolio, whatever the policy says.

questions.stem: Which step in the allocation process usually determines the final answer?
choices: The constraints — liquidity needs, policy limits, governance tolerance and horizon
rationales: Expected returns matter enormously and are nearly unknowable, which is why weeks spent refining them adds little.
Correct. An unconstrained optimiser recommends portfolios no institution could hold. Once realistic constraints are applied, the feasible set is small and the constraints have effectively chosen.
Technique affects the answer at the margin and less than the constraint set does.
Correlations matter and are estimated from history, and they are still applied within the constraints.
questions.explanation: Which is a useful reordering of effort: define what the portfolio genuinely cannot do — sell nothing for ten years, survive a 35% drawdown — before optimising within it. That work is neglected because it is uncomfortable rather than difficult.

questions.stem: A private strategy returns 10% with 8% reported volatility, against a 3% risk-free rate. What is its reported Sharpe ratio? Two decimal places.
questions.explanation: On unsmoothed volatility of 16% the same returns give 0.44 — still better than public equity's 0.31, and by a plausible margin rather than an implausible one. The correction does not eliminate the case for the allocation; it right-sizes it.

questions.stem: Same 10% return and 3% risk-free rate, but unsmoothed volatility is 16%. What is the corrected Sharpe ratio? Two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Half the reported figure, from correcting one input. An optimiser given 0.88 and 0.44 produces very different portfolios, and only one of those numbers describes a series that was actually traded.

questions.stem: "Private equity diversifies a portfolio because its correlation with public equity is low." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — the low measured correlation is largely a product of smoothed quarterly marks; unsmoothed, private equity is levered equity with high correlation to public equity
False — private equity has negative correlation with public equity
True — the measured correlation is genuinely low
False — because correlation is irrelevant to diversification
rationales: Correct. Once the estimation lag is removed, the correlation rises substantially. The businesses share an economy, a financing environment and an exit market.
It is positive and high on corrected data.
It is measured as low, and the measurement reflects the valuation process rather than the exposure.
Correlation is central to diversification, which is why the artefact matters so much.
questions.explanation: The real case for private equity is the illiquidity premium, access to a different opportunity set and control — all defensible. Diversification is the one claim the data does not support, and it is the one most often made because it is the one an optimiser rewards.

questions.stem: A pension fund states a twenty-year horizon but reviews managers against annual benchmarks and has terminated three managers after two bad years each. What is its effective horizon?
choices: Twenty years, as stated in the policy
About two years — the revealed tolerance, which is the constraint that actually binds
rationales: The stated horizon is a policy statement contradicted by the behaviour.
Correct. Revealed preference is the operative constraint. A portfolio built for twenty years and governed on two will be dismantled in the first sustained drawdown.
Nothing here indicates five years, and the terminations indicate two.
It is determinable from the behaviour, which is more informative than the document.
questions.explanation: The productive response is to state the real tolerance and build within it, rather than building for the stated horizon and discovering the real one in a bad year. A smaller allocation to illiquid assets that survives is worth more than a larger one that gets sold at the bottom.

questions.stem: What single check should precede any optimisation involving private assets?
choices: Verifying the expected return assumptions with a consultant
Computing the autocorrelation of each private return series, and unsmoothing where it is high
Adding more asset classes to the opportunity set
rationales: Expected returns are the least knowable input and consultants' estimates are also estimates.
Correct. High autocorrelation identifies smoothing, and the correction changes the volatility and correlation inputs that drive the whole allocation.
A longer sample of smoothed data is still smoothed.
More asset classes with distorted inputs compounds the problem.
questions.explanation: It is one calculation on data already in hand, and it changes the answer rather than refining it. That combination — cheap, decisive, rarely done — makes it the highest-return check in the whole allocation process.
